entry.title: Meurisse
entry.summary: Proyecto por AUGE Design con 17 imágenes.
entry.content:
Autor(es): AUGE Design, Miriam Frescura, Federico Landini, Stefano Romano, Reem Radhi, Sara Bigagli

/identity /packaging

MEURISSE

CLIENT
Meurisse is Belgium’s first chocolate company, with a rich heritage dating back to 1845. With a long history of craftsmanship and a familiar visual identity, the brand continues to explore new ways of expressing its story while staying connected to the elements that customers have grown accustomed to.

ASSIGNMENT
The branding system started with a simple idea: keep the arched logo and frame that customers have grown accustomed to, but give them a more meaningful role. The aim was to bring more presence, elegance and purpose to these familiar elements, creating a visual identity that could tell the story of Meurisse’s travels while celebrating its long-standing heritage.

SOLUTION & PROCESS
What was once a simple outlined window and a classically arched logo becomes something with a little more presence, elegance and purpose. The arch takes a new, stair-cased form, giving the logo the feeling of a movie headline announcing the beginning of a great adventure. The arch and frame become the little stage on which Meurisse’s travels unfold, holding stories from the many places he has visited along the way.

Across the different chocolate formats, the frame changes character, becoming a postcard or a wrapped souvenir from somewhere far away. Every pack carries the line ‘exploring taste since 1845’, accompanied by refreshed archival symbols such as the CM mark, small reminders that although Meurisse is always travelling forward, he has been on the journey for quite some time. And so the chocolates continue on their way, aboard the Orient Express, carefully packed, labelled and ready for their next destination.

entry.title: Bayard Kids
entry.summary: Proyecto por 🟥⬜️ Graphéine con 32 imágenes.
entry.content:
Autor(es): 🟥⬜️ Graphéine

Bayard Kids
Bayard Jeunesse

For 60 years, Bayard Jeunesse has accompanied children and teenagers through their discoveries, learning experiences and countless adventures. From Petit Ours Brun to Ariol, from Pomme d’Api to Phosphore, the brand has helped generations of young readers grow up through an incredible diversity of stories, characters and imaginary worlds.

Today, stories are no longer told on paper alone. Books, magazines, apps, podcasts, animated series… Bayard Jeunesse has become a multimedia brand, exploring every avenue of creative content for young audiences. Whether through a magazine or an animated series, the ambition remains the same: to inspire laughter, play, curiosity and reflection, helping children grow and find their own voice by nurturing a love of reading, a hunger for knowledge and a thirst to discover the world.

In a landscape dominated by Disney, Netflix and YouTube, Bayard Jeunesse is determined to champion an ambitious vision of children’s content and proudly stand by its promise: “Growing in confidence.”

How do you bring this galaxy of creative worlds together under one brand without compromising their individual identities? This was the challenge at the heart of our mission: to evolve the brand identity and strengthen the Bayard Jeunesse masterbrand, giving it greater character, visibility and consistency, from print to screen, in France and around the world.
A New Symbol

To complement this new symbol, we redesigned the wordmark. Proportions were rebalanced, shapes simplified and letterforms given greater weight to create a visual signature that is bold, approachable and expressive.

The return of the word “Jeunesse” clearly reaffirms the brand’s focus on young audiences. Designed to work across one or two lines, the wordmark adapts seamlessly to the requirements of different formats and media.

The combination of Bayard’s iconic yellow, deep black and geometric shapes creates an instantly recognisable identity, equally at home on a book cover or a smartphone screen.
One B, a Thousand Stories to Tell

Petit Ours Brun, SamSam, Ariol, Anatole Latuile… Bayard Jeunesse brings together a wide variety of characters and visual worlds. The challenge was not to standardise this diversity, but to give it a unifying symbol.

The new wordmark acts as a shared signature, bold enough to identify the publisher yet discreet enough to let the illustrations, characters and stories take centre stage. Whether placed at the bottom of a book cover, on magazines or across different collections, it creates a visual connection between creations that each retain their own distinct personality.

In short, we set out to design a brand that brings stories together without ever stealing the spotlight.
Growing Up with Confidence

A brand positioning built around a simple promise with a big ambition. Growing up means having a thousand questions to ask adults. It means discovering, trying, making mistakes and starting all over again. To support children through their first steps and their greatest discoveries, Bayard Jeunesse places trust and confidence at the heart of its promise.

Above all, it’s about the confidence children develop in themselves, in others and in the world around them. A belief that spans generations and finds expression in every form of creative content, from books to animated series.

Because it’s not just about telling stories. It’s also about giving children the tools to understand the world, nurture their curiosity and forge their own path.
Used independently on certain applications, the wordmark has been redesigned to give the brand a stronger visual presence and a more distinctive personality. The custom lettering builds on the geometric foundations of the previously used typeface, Gilroy. Its playful and approachable character has been preserved, while the black has been made bolder and the ascenders and descenders shortened, allowing the wordmark to work effectively on either one or two lines.
Today, a children’s brand needs to move seamlessly from books to apps, from magazine covers to animated series.

Designed to work across this wide range of formats, the new identity combines simplicity, legibility and versatility. The B becomes a distinctive visual symbol that can stand on its own, while the complete wordmark reinforces Bayard Jeunesse’s presence across all its productions.

An identity that preserves the strength of traditional publishing while embracing the codes and conventions of digital media.
The wordmark is placed at the bottom of book covers across the various collections, while the full version is used in a vertical layout on all magazines.
Bayard Kids: Stories Without Borders

With Bayard Kids, the identity continues its expansion internationally. Built on the same graphic principles as Bayard Jeunesse, this adaptation retains the iconic B and an instantly recognisable typographic signature. The visual system adapts to different markets and supports a range of content with a particular focus on animation, digital media and audiovisual productions.

Two expressions of the same brand, sharing the same spirit of discovery and the same ambition: to help children broaden their horizons and explore the world. An identity that grows alongside its audiences, its stories and its ever-expanding creative possibilities.

entry.title: GEOTHERMAL LAYERS — Iceland
entry.summary: Abstract aerial studies of Icelandic geothermal terrain, where pale blue water, mineral crusts and altered clay form delicate channels, cracks and layered textures across the volcanic ground.
entry.content:
Autor(es): Jan Erik Waider

Abstract aerial studies of Icelandic geothermal terrain, where pale blue water, mineral crusts and altered clay form delicate channels, cracks and layered textures across the volcanic ground.

GEOTHERMAL LAYERS – Iceland

What drew me to these surfaces was their unexpectedly restrained palette: pale blue water, white and grey mineral crusts, soft brown clay and fragments of dark volcanic ground. Seen from very close above, channels, cracks, ridges and deposits begin to read less like a geothermal field and more like an abstract map.

The lighter areas feel almost delicate, while the darker sections shift into something much more organic and unsettling. Their layered textures, swollen edges and irregular forms have an almost biomechanical, alien quality. That contrast fascinated me most: within the same landscape, the surface can move from soft and minimal to dense, strange and almost otherworldly, all shaped by water, minerals, heat and continuous geothermal activity.

entry.title: 2026 Brand New Conference Identity
entry.summary: Proyecto por UnderConsideration LLC con 83 imágenes.
entry.content:
Autor(es): UnderConsideration LLC

This past September 17 & 18 we celebrated the fifteenth edition of the Brand New Conference in Nashville, TN, with the wildest bachelorette party theme ever applied to a design conference in the history of our industry and we can say that with the highest degree of confidence and by embracing all of the hyperbole that comes with saying something is the most ever of something given that literally no design conference has ever dressed up like this given that there is no rational reason for why any design conference would ever present itself as a bachelorette party, which is exactly why WE did. So how in the yee-haw did we arrive at this theme?
A False Start
Despite how rich they are as sources of inspiration our first challenge was finding another angle to Nashville that wasn’t country music or Hatch Show Print because we did that in 2016 and an initial round of online research revealed one possible theme: Radio. Although still associated with country music, another Nashville musical landmark is the Grand Ole Opry, a live country-music show that, having started in 1927, is the longest-running radio broadcast in U.S. history. The show is made available to listeners by local radio station, WSM, that, in 1941 was the first U.S. broadcaster to receive a commercial FM license. So vintage radio-related graphics felt like a sure bet but we needed some actual reference sources and we headed down to Nashville to visit the Grand Ole Opry House and the modern-day WSM Radio station that sits directly in front of it that happens to feature a new permanent exhibit called “Behind The Airwaves: Discover The Radio Home Of The Opry”. We could have not asked for a more perfect source of material. We took a hundred photos of cool radio-y stuff and left Opryland fairly satisfied.

<div>Photos from the exhibit “Behind The Airwaves: Discover The Radio Home Of The Opry”.</div>

We drove into Nashville, checked into our hotel, and headed out for a cup of coffee to reassess our findings and decide the next steps on how to activate our radio theme. Somewhat quickly, we had the disappointing realization that this was not it. Yes, vintage radio graphics and all kinds of 1960s typographic shenanigans would have been cool but we could not find the spin to make it special.
How we got our Groove Back
On the walk from the hotel to the coffee shop, somewhere around 3:00 pm on a Saturday, we walked past endless group of women ready to party… some for the sake of it, some for bachelorette parties, all in what seemed like a standard-issue uniform for the occasion that included denim shorts, cowboy boots, tops with fringe, and somewhere — anywhere — sparks of bedazzlement. Over the years, it turns out, Nashville has become one of the top destinations for bachelorette parties and a whole cottage industry has sprung around it to complement the already epic nightlife and picture-perfect backdrop of Broadway and its tireless honky tonk bars.
As we sat in the coffee shop somewhat defeated, we jokingly said that instead of a conference we should just throw a bachelorette party — probably more fun and less stressful. We laughed it off until we realized that that was it. That’s what we were going to hang our proverbial (cowboy) hat on as the theme of this year’s conference identity: A bachelorette party. Knowing it was a wild idea very much outside of our comfort zone, we shook on it and headed out to Broadway to find more inspiration. Broadway delivered.

<div>No shortage of inspiration on Broadway.</div>

The Moodboard
Satisfied with our field research we went back to the office and did what any good bridesmaid in charge of a bachelorette party would do, which is to put together a Pinterest board. (For the record, we’ve NEVER done a moodboard before for any conference or client project.) To our surprise and delight there is a whole online ecosystem devoted not just to bachelorette parties but bachelorette parties in Nashville that marries the obligatory pink hues and script lettering of the industry with the giddy-up clichés of the city, featuring more cowboy hats and rhinestones than you can shake feather boas at. The moodboard helped us define some starting points for the identity: One, it had to be pink. Two, it had to use a cheesy script font. And three, it had to integrate something cowboy-y. It also proved to be a well of ideas for many of the identity elements, materials, and applications.

<div>The official 2026 BNConf <a href="https://pin.it/5lLwYvsrj" target="_blank" rel="nofollow">moodboard</a>.</div>

Identity Elements
The first design decision we made, which was a no-brainer, was to select pink as the primary color complemented and contrasted by black and white. We also introduced “denim” as a color-slash-texture that could be used in digital and other print applications given that denim, as you will see further below, plays a key role in our bachelorette party theme. Lastly, we landed on “shiny” as another color-slash-texture that could be brought into the identity in different ways.

<div>Color palette.</div>

For typography, the first typeface we recruited was F37 Roy, designed by Alec Tear. We didn’t necessarily want to use another woodtype slab serif given that we made that the foundation of the 2016 identity but it really is an unavoidable reference. For the “cheesy script” we decided to not go full cheese and instead chose Gratitude Smooth Script by Alejandro Paul and Kathy Milici, which had the perfect balance of penmanship and exuberance without being too Live-Laugh-Love-y. In supporting roles we have Stilson because no bachelorette party invitation or party favor can exist without a Didone serif and Balto, an American Gothic that would not have been out of place in the good old days of woodtype.

<div>Typography.<br></div>

A recurring element in our moodboard was the various sentences spelled out using mylar balloons, a staple of any celebration but a particularly kitschy one for bachelorette parties and, even though we already had four different typefaces in play, we could not resist spelling out “BNCONF” in mylar balloons.

<div>Mylar balloons.<br></div>

For digital purposes we wanted to have the balloons in motion, swaying in the wind and bumping against each other. This could have probably been done in 3D or *shivers* AI but, of course, we had to do it the analog way. We took our 40-inch-tall balloons and a canister of helium and headed to the studio of our small town’s star photographer, Anna Powell Denton, to capture footage of the balloons being pushed around by a fan and a leaf blower behind the scenes.
One of our favorite pieces of bachelorette party ornamentation turned out to be the rhinestone pearl letters used in the very popular “Bride” cowboy hat so, to add yet another typographic element, we ordered “BNCONF”, “2026”, and a couple of hearts to photograph and use in digital applications. (At the time we didn’t know it but these letters ended up making a second appearance in the physical materials.)

<div>“Bride” cowboy hat inspiration from our moodboard and the rhinestone pearl letters in their natural state.</div>

<div>Rhinestone pearl letters ready for use. Somewhere along the process we determined these should only ever be used on top of the denim texture (and never on white or pink).</div>

To help frame, divide, and tie up all of the elements across layouts we developed a small collection of repeatable patterns inspired by bachelorette party invitations, chief among them the “scallop” pattern that became an integral element. A strip of fringe that can be used to transition from pink to white. A squiggly line with thicks and thins matching Gratitude Script that makes recurring appearances as an underline. Lastly, a simple diamond-esque shape that can be repeated in small sizes for a sparkly effect.

<div>Patterns and dividers.</div>

Digital Applications
With all of the elements defined, the first application was the website and there is no big explanation needed here… we used everything. Ditto for the Instagram content and the slides that keep the show flowing.
Opening Titles and Speaker Intros
Like the previous fours years, we enlisted our team of GEO for motion and Norbert Herber for custom music to create the opening titles and three similar-but-different speaker introductions. The general direction for the sound and motion was “Honky Tonk meets Hyperpop Party Mix”.
Tote Bags
As mentioned in one of the opening paragraphs, one of the most popular items of clothing to wear when partying in Nashville’s downtown area is the denim short. To be specific: The very short and very tight denim short. As a staple of any good bachelorette party we decided to honor the short shorts by transforming them into tote bags. Realizing that it would be the item that would take the longest and require the most steps, this is where we started this year’s production.

The first step was securing 800 denim shorts. At first we assumed we would have to drive to every large second-hand store in the state of Indiana (and possibly Illinois and Kentucky) to slowly buy what we needed. Luckily we found a wholesale vendor in Florida who had 700 in stock and we purchased all of their inventory while the extra 100 came from a couple of separate visits to local second-hand stores. (Whew!) Each short had to be inspected for any tags, missing buttons, or major defects and we ironed anything that was far too wrinkled. We then separated them into two groups, one for the XS, S, and M sizes and one for the L, XL, and XXL sizes so that we could create two separate versions for the artwork to avoid having tiny logos in huge shorts or huge logos in tiny shorts since there was no magic mid-point size that would work across all of the shapes and sizes.

For the design on the tote bags, we wanted to keep things simple so that the short would be the hero. We opted for a slightly jumbled “BNC” composition in F37 Roy in pink and a rhinestone version of “Nashville” in Gratitude Smooth Script (which required “redrawing” the word one dot at a time and maintain the delicate script flow as much as possible). To apply both elements we used a heat press so that we could get opaque, bright, pink letters and actual (cheap) rhinestone transfers unto the denim (which is not kind to most other transferring methods we tested).

<div>Small and large versions of the artwork for the tote bags. For the record, the small version wasn’t just scaled down, it had to be redrawn as the rhinestones are the same physical dimensions for both variations.<br></div>

Once branded, it was time to turn the shorts into bags by sewing the leg openings shut. Shorts were organized by colors so that we could match the thread as closes as possible so that it wouldn’t be visible. To sew them, each short had to be pinned in strategic positions to hold it in place before putting it through the sewing machine, which meant that all those pins also had to be taken out and since we were already being surgical about it we made sure to trim off any extra thread. The last step was attaching the purse chains to the belt loops which was done on site the day before the event.

<div>Tote bags.<br></div>

<div>Tote bag setup for check-in so attendees could choose their preferred one.<br></div>

<div>Tote bags in action.<br></div>

Programs
The next item on the agenda was the program because we also knew it was going to require plenty of steps and lead time. For this one, our idea was that it should feel like a bachelorette party slash bride-to-be scrapbook or journal with a lot of frilly stuff glued on the cover. For the “frilly stuff” we ordered about 30 different styles of ribbons — different materials, patterns, contours, and shapes — all within our color palette of pink, black, white, and “shiny” to wrap from the front cover to the back cover in multiple compositions and combinations. To “brand” the cover we went back to the pearl rhinestone letters and ordered a ton of “B”s, “N”s, and “C”s with self-adhesive backing. To make this work with our schedule we decided to create a slip cover so that we didn’t have to wait for the program to be printed and there was also no smooth way of attaching the ribbons directly to a bound book.

<div>Program structure.<br></div>

With the ribbons cut, there were two different methods to attach them to the slip cover. The wider, solid ribbons were able to accommodate a strip of double-stick tape in the back while the thinner and/or oddly-shaped ribbons had to be glued. Each attachment method required a different process too where the ones that required glue (shown first below) were the “easy” ones while the ones with the double-stick tape had to be applied on a funky “jig” we constructed that looks like a little house which allowed us to apply them with the slip cover slightly folded because if applied flat it created too much tension on the slip cover and it would make it buck. After both the glued and double-stick-taped ribbons were attached, their ends had to be tucked into the slits and taped to the inside to secure them in place.

<div>Programs.<br></div>

<div>Front and back covers without slip cover.<br></div>

<div>Slip cover.<br></div>

<div>Program setup for check-in so attendees could choose their preferred one.<br></div>

Badges
The very first idea we had in that fateful coffee shop meeting was to replace traditional name badges — well, as traditional as ours tend to be, which is not traditional at all — with bride-to-be and bridesmaid sashes in all their cheesy, satin glory. We considered ordering off-the-shelf sashes with one of the hundreds of vendors that provide this novelty item but we did need some conference branding on them and some flexibility in the placement of the artwork so we ordered some spools of the material and cut it to size to then send to our local silkscreen printer who battled valiantly with the squiggly fabric.
The main challenge with the sashes was how to integrate and apply each attendee’s personal details. Given there was no easy way to do so directly on the sash we turned once more to our heat press — unquestionably this year’s MVP of equipment — but unlike the previous uses where we could order a bunch of the same design these all had to be individualized so we found a transfer paper that we could print on with our basic color printer and run through our laser-cutter, which allowed us to get a little more adventuresome with a funky scallop holding shape.

<div>Badges-slash-sashes.<br></div>

<div>Sashes in action.</div>

T-shirts
Since we spent a good deal of time rhinestone-izing the “Nashville” script we figured we would get some additional mileage out of it in the attendee t-shirts. Also, in case it’s not evident: The t-shirts are VERY pink.

<div>T-shirts<br></div>

Staff Getups
Usually, our volunteers get a t-shirt similar to the one attendees get but in a different color and they would say “Staff” somewhere but we had a rare opportunity to do something a little more unique for them this year. We ordered them each a bitchin’ denim vest, which we tricked out with the leftover pink “BNC”s and “Nashville” rhinestones. Underneath, a simple white t-shirt with “Staff” and the event name heat-pressed on the sleeves.

<div>Staff t-shirts and vests.<br></div>

<div>Staff in action.<br></div>

Stage
Two other materials we wanted to play with — feather boas and disco ball mirrors — but had not found a use for were the perfect solution to decorate the typography on stage and add plenty of texture and dimensionality with relative ease. The feather boas could easily be twisted to flow with the script and be doubled up to echo the thicks and thins while the disco ball mirrors could easily be applied to the broader mass of F37 Roy.

<div>Various views of the stage letters. You can right click and open any image in a new tab/window for a bigger view.<br></div>

<div>Podium decked with mylar balloons.<br></div>

The Fits
Since we are part of the show, we always make sure our fits are on brand and this was probably one of the most fun years to shop for. For each day we traded who got to wear a denim-dominant outfit while the other added the pink and white bursts of color. The knit sweater with the scallop pattern on the bottom could not have been a more on-brand find.

<div>Fits for each day. (It looks like we are hating every minute on stage but we actually smile a lot… these were just the few pictures that had our full bodies together.)<br></div>

The End
From the very beginning we knew this identity wasn’t going to be everyone’s cup of tea and we purposely leaned hard on the cringe factor but if there is one thing we would love for you to take away from this year’s identity and materials, aside from the fact that pink rocks and the obvious lesson to get out of your comfort zones is that, at a time when both our professional work and our personal life are in a constant state of optimizing for the literal and metaphorical algorithm, sometimes the right solution requires an irrational approach, that sometimes the right user experience is created by the wrong user interface, and that sometimes the appropriate answer demands the silliest questions. Life is too short to play it safe all the time. Giddy-up before it’s too late.
Get yours!

entry.title: Imagination Day 12
entry.summary: Imagination Day is a true celebration of creativity — an event that brings together visionaries, makers, and speakers from around the world. With each edition, its ambition and momentum continued to grow, but the visual identity could no longer keep up with the pace of the industry. That’s why we set out to create an entirely new visual language: bold, flexible, and expansive enough to capture the diversity of today’s creative landscape. The result is a complete rebrand, a set of fresh visual assets, and a new website that give Imagination Day the energy to move confidently into the years ahead.

Coatlicue-Tonantzin is the mother goddess of nature, death, and the mother of the gods in the Mesoamerican worldview, particularly within the Mexica tradition.
As the archetypal great mother, she embodies the feminine principle that gives life within nature. For this project we worked with interior and furniture designer Andrés Gutiérrez, who—guided by a vivid color palette inspired by Mesoamerican cosmology—selected marbles, volcanic stones, and textured materials for building a bar inspired by the mother goddess of the Mexica pantheon. Within that chromatic range and the primordial creation myth, we developed a graphic identity based on these concepts and on the furniture and interior design created by Andrés Gutiérrez, drawing on elements such as the serpent, femininity, and maternity, as well as Mexican aesthetics associated with the goddess Coatlicue-Tonantzin. 
To produce the graphic pieces—stationery, the menu, digital applications, etc.—we referenced Mesoamerican codices, glyphs, and motifs inspired by pre-Hispanic Náhuatl aesthetics. The company’s primary typeface incorporates motifs linked to maternity in Mexica culture, such as forms that evoke breasts, square and pyramidal structures; the letter N is inspired by the distinctive boot-like shape found in Mexico.

entry.title: DOLIVING apartment branding
entry.summary: Proyecto por ONNFF™ ART&DESIGN con 25 imágenes.
entry.content:
Autor(es): ONNFF™ ART&DESIGN

DOLIVING apartment Brand Identity Design

有度里公寓的品牌设计，从居所这一朴素命题展开。中文标识外嵌房屋轮廓，像边界，也像庇护，成为贯穿始终的图形表达。围绕这一核心，我们延伸出一套完整的品牌触点：室内标识与导视、手提袋、信封、单页，以及房子形状的盒子和杯子等日常物件。品牌因此不只停留在平面，而是进入居住者的行走、取用与停留之间。天蓝与草绿构成主色，一面呼应天空的开阔，一面呼应草地的自然，整体传达舒适、自由、轻松的居住状态。

The identity for DOLIVING Apartment begins with a simple idea: dwelling. A house outline frames the Chinese wordmark—at once a boundary and a shelter—and becomes the recurring graphic language of the brand. Around this core, a complete set of touchpoints was developed: interior signage and wayfinding, tote bags, envelopes, leaflets, as well as the house-shaped box and cup. The brand therefore moves beyond graphic surfaces and enters the daily paths of residents—walking, reaching, pausing. Sky blue and grass green form the primary palette, echoing the openness of the sky and the natural ease of a meadow. The overall character is comfortable, free, and relaxed.

entry.title: Faminto
entry.summary: Proyecto por Another Collective con 26 imágenes.
entry.content:
Autor(es): Another Collective




Before there were recipes, there was hunger. Before there were kitchens, there was fire. Faminto was born from that almost primal instinct: the meeting of meat and flame, in a place where everything is shaped by iron and fire.

This identity makes no attempt to tame that hunger. It embraces it through a bold, direct and no-frills visual language, built around one of our oldest relationships: the one between animal, fire and those who gather around it. At the heart of the visual system, an ancestral figure echoes the earliest images left on stone, like a mark carried through time.

Textures and organic forms extend this raw, instinctive world, while the typographic language brings structure and a more contemporary rhythm. The contrast between the irregularity of the graphic elements and the precision of the typography gives the identity a strong, distinctive presence without taking away what feels most spontaneous about Faminto.

Rather than reinventing what has always made sense, the identity takes the brand back to the essentials: fire, meat and the hunger that brings people to the table. It asks neither permission nor forgiveness. It arrives hungry and gets straight to the point.
